facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989 the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The demonstrators gathered at the Ayios Kassianos school in Nicosia.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 3 January 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

The UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
The UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by the United Nations Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.

The UN Secretary General stated that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the women demonstrators.

After United Nations soldiers had shouted a warning to the demonstrators not to advance further, the applicant was seized by the hair by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The applicant was beaten and assaulted by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The beating of the applicant was inflicted with electrical batons by 3 or 4 policemen all over the applicant's body, in particular the head and back.
The applicant was dragged to a small, stiflingly hot room in which other demonstrators were also being held.
One of the female prisoners, Mrs Vrahimi (application no. 16078/90), was beaten in front of the other detainees at the Pavlides Garage.
Later on 20 July 1989, after being subjected to a body search, the applicant was taken to a court which remanded her in custody for two days.
The judge at the Nicosia District Court asked the applicant and the other accused whether they wanted legal representation.
As a result of the applicant and the other accused refusing to accept a lawyer not registered with the bar association of the Republic of Cyprus, they were not assisted by a lawyer at trial.
The interpretation into Greek at the Nicosia District Court trial was poor and did not cover all the words used by the witnesses and the parties.
Each time an accused tried to speak and give an explanation at the Nicosia District Court trial, she was interrupted.

The English translation of the Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 23 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law No. 5/72.

The English translation of the Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 23 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as five or more persons assembled with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conducting themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(b) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who commits in his presence any offence punishable with imprisonment.
Chapter 155, section 14(1)(c) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who obstructs a police officer while in the execution of his duty.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'TRNC'.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The applicant was beaten and assaulted by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.
The beating of the applicant was inflicted with electrical batons by 3 or 4 policemen all over the applicant's body, in particular the head and back.
One of the blows to the applicant caused a painful injury to the applicant's right arm and elbow, with loss of blood.
The applicant was dragged to a small, stiflingly hot room in which other demonstrators were also being held.
The applicant was forced to sit on the floor at the Pavlides Garage.
The toilet facilities at the Pavlides Garage were filthy.
A crowd gathered outside the Pavlides Garage was swearing, shouting abuse and threats, and throwing stones, some of which came through the corrugated iron roof.
One of the female prisoners, Mrs Vrahimi (application no. 16078/90), was beaten in front of the other detainees at the Pavlides Garage.
The conditions of detention at the Ortakeuy prison were appalling and the cell was unbearably hot.
During the night at the Ortakeuy prison, the applicant and the other detainees were constantly checked and counted by the guards and as a result were unable to sleep.
The applicant went on hunger strike while detained at the Ortakeuy prison.
The judge at the Nicosia District Court asked the applicant and the other accused whether they wanted legal representation.
As a result of the applicant and the other accused refusing to accept a lawyer not registered with the bar association of the Republic of Cyprus, they were not assisted by a lawyer at trial.
The interpretation into Greek at the Nicosia District Court trial was poor and did not cover all the words used by the witnesses and the parties.
Each time an accused tried to speak and give an explanation at the Nicosia District Court trial, she was interrupted.
The applicant tried to explain her position regarding the penknife to the judge but was not allowed to.
The applicant showed her bandaged arm in order to complain about the beating she had suffered, but an officer replied that she could have injured herself by falling down.

On 22 July 1989, the Nicosia District Court ordered the applicant to enter into a recognizance of 1,000,000 Turkish liras as a guarantee that she would not commit further breaches of the peace for a period of one year.

Most of the accused, including the applicant, were sentenced to 2 days' imprisonment and a fine of 50 Cypriot pounds (approximately 85 euros), with five additional days in prison in default of payment within 24 hours.
